articles.title: Native, React Native or Flutter: Which Mobile Build Fits Your Product
articles.excerpt: Somewhere near the start of a mobile project, a decision gets made that quietly shapes everything after it: whether to build twice, build once in a cross-platform framework, or pick a middle path. It…
articles.body: Somewhere near the start of a mobile project, a decision gets made that quietly shapes everything after it: whether to build twice, build once in a cross-platform framework, or pick a middle path. It rarely gets the attention it deserves, because it looks like a technical preference. It is closer to a business decision about budget, timeline, and who will maintain the thing in two years. Here is how the three common routes compare, and who each one tends to suit. Native iOS and Android, built separately This is two codebases, two teams or one team working twice, and two release cycles. It is the most expensive route and the slowest to reach feature parity, because every change happens twice.

articles.body: I'm Dmitry, a Canadian rider. I built ALLR (allr.io), a price-comparison site for motorcycle gear. No store pays us, and this post has no affiliate links. It is about the two parts that took longest to get right: finding the same product in every store, and working out what it really costs when the store is not in your country. The problem A helmet listed at 339.99 EUR in Germany, 549.99 USD in the US and 715 CAD in Ontario cannot be compared by looking at the numbers. For a Canadian buyer the price is: item (in CAD) + shipping + import duty + customs brokerage and the item part is itself a conversion, sometimes after removing a tax. I call that total the landed cost.

articles.title: LangGraph.js Runs on a Class Named Pregel. Google's 2010 Paper Explains Your Graph
articles.excerpt: Book: AI That Plans The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claud…
articles.body: Book: AI That Plans The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub Call .compile() on a LangGraph.js StateGraph and follow the class chain. CompiledStateGraph extends CompiledGraph , and CompiledGraph extends Pregel . That is the runtime that executes your agent, and the LangGraph docs say plainly where the name comes from: Google's Pregel, a system for parallel graph computation. The paper is Pregel: A System for Large-Scale Graph Processing by Malewicz and six co-authors at Google, published at SIGMOD 2010 , pages 135–146. It was built for huge graphs spread across a cluster.

articles.title: Pattern Guardrails Under Mutation: A Three-Metric Evaluation of Two Agent Safety Layers
articles.excerpt: Abstract. I built two agent systems guarded by pattern matching: a tool-using support agent behind a regex-style injection detector, and a SQL agent behind a validate-then-approve gate. I tested how t…
articles.body: Abstract. I built two agent systems guarded by pattern matching: a tool-using support agent behind a regex-style injection detector, and a SQL agent behind a validate-then-approve gate. I tested how those layers hold against systematically mutated attacks, and what the defence costs in false refusals and lost completion. I mutated my seeds deterministically (147 agent-guardrail cases; 84 SQL attacks, 13 benign controls), added an indirect-injection scenario suite, and scored three metrics: attack success rate (ASR), false-refusal rate (FRR), and completion under attack. Surface-form mutations were blocked almost perfectly; encoded payloads (base64, ROT13, leetspeak, zero-width, homoglyphs) collapsed the pattern layer — 0 of 24 runs blocked per class.
articles.author: Tushar Kumar

articles.title: How to Connect AI Coding Agents to a Governed Delivery Workflow
articles.excerpt: When a coding agent can edit multiple files, run commands, or open a pull request, code generation is only part of the problem. The team also needs to know which requirement the work serves, who owns…
articles.body: When a coding agent can edit multiple files, run commands, or open a pull request, code generation is only part of the problem. The team also needs to know which requirement the work serves, who owns it, what approvals apply, and where delivery stands. A practical approach is to treat the agent as an execution participant, not as the system of record for the work. Keep requirements, tasks, dependencies, statuses, and approval rules in shared project workflows; then choose an agent tool that fits the coding environment and deployment constraints. Map the workflow before choosing a tool Start by tracing one piece of work from its requirement to delivery. Identify where people record the requirement, assign ownership, track dependencies, review changes, and report status.

articles.title: New 'Star Trek: The Original Voyages' book traces the stellar legacy of the bold sci-fi brand
articles.excerpt: Keep the 60th anniversary party going with this visual salute to the series that launched a legacy
articles.body: "Star Trek" celebrated its diamond anniversary last month, marking 60 years since it first aired on NBC on Sept. 8, 1966. There were a bunch of Trekkie-themed celebrations and news stories over September, including festive documentaries , special screenings , tributes, parade floats , interviews, and even a Galileo shuttle story. Now, publishers Penguin Random House and Ten Speed Press are releasing " Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History " on Nov. 10, 2026. This coffee table book promises unprecedented exploration of the pioneering space fantasy television series and enduring pop culture property that bolstered the space race and ignited sci-fi audiences' imaginations by taking us to strange new worlds and civilizations in the final frontier.

articles.title: Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II EVO FE (APO) lens review — how good is this budget lens for astrophotography?
articles.excerpt: The Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II FE (APO) is an inexpensive prime that works well for astrophotography thanks to its focal length and maximum aperture.
articles.body: Key specs Type: Full-frame prime lens Focal length: 35 mm Maximum aperture: f/1.8 Lens mount: Sony FE & Nikon Z Weight: 12.52 oz / 355 g Dimensions: 3.33 x 4.37 in / 69 x 76 mm Filter thread: 58 mm Release date: April 2026 Budget primes can be, surprisingly, excellent choices for photographers shooting all subjects. It’s all too easy to get carried away with the best specs, such as a large maximum aperture and impressive optical design often seen in more expensive options. But affordable lenses like the Viltrox AF 35mm f/1.8 II FE (APO) have the potential to impress and delight in equal measure. The 35mm f/1.8 is a compact and lightweight lens offering a reasonably fast maximum aperture, making it a prime candidate for astrophotography.

articles.title: NASA’s CHAPEA Crew “Returns” to Earth
articles.excerpt: The four-member Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) crew poses outside for the first time in more than a year following the end of their simulated Mars journey on Oct. 31, 2026. Cr…
articles.body: NASA/James Blair The four-member Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) crew poses outside for the first time in more than a year following the end of their simulated Mars journey on Oct. 31, 2026. Crew members Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right) spent more than a year testing systems, maintaining crops, managing limited resources and communication delays, conducting extravehicular activities and more in efforts to help NASA better understand how crews adapt to long-duration stays. Insights from their experiences will help NASA design its future Moon Base and plan for missions on Mars. Image credit: NASA/James Blair
